items.abstract: Even as increasing research has sought to identify consumers’ perceptions of the uses of corporate social responsibility (CSR) during negative marketing events, a clear understanding of the ethical foundations and potential implications for business ethics research remains missing. To address this gap, a bibliometric analysis of 121 peer-reviewed articles, published in 69 journals between 2004 and 2024, traces the evolution and diversification of CSR research in negative marketing contexts. The findings reveal two primary research streams, pertaining to corporate associations and crisis communication, which in turn encompass four thematic clusters: CSR buffering effects, CSR-based crisis communication, CSR crises, and CSR backfiring. A longitudinal assessment further indicates that though this research stream draws from various disciplinary perspectives, it has not yet engaged meaningfully with normative ethical theories. In an effort to advance business ethics literature, the proposed research agenda highlights key ethical considerations and pathways for integrating normative ethical frameworks into CSR research involving negative marketing events.
items.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Negative Marketing Events: The Overlooked Role of Normative Ethics

items.abstract: Abstract The article compares two ways to think about the implicit structure of systems studied in pure mathematics. The first approach specifies implicit structure in terms of formal languages, relying on a model-theoretic notion of definability. The second approach defines the notion in terms of invariance criteria. The structural features of a given system are often considered to be properties which are invariant under specific transformations of the system. In the paper, I analyze these two approaches to implicit structure in terms of invariance and definability conditions by drawing to the field of finite geometry. I then explore their formal relationship in the framework of relational algebra, based on the concepts of Galois closures and Krasner algebras. Finally, I examine the equivalence of mathematical systems with respect to their implicit structure in terms of the model-theoretic notion of bi-interpretability.
items.title: Two Ways to Think About (Implicit) Structure

items.abstract: This paper outlines a naturalistic yet non-deflationary account of subjective experience. I advance five theses which, when taken together, offer an account which retains the reality of subjective experience in a way that’s convivial to the scientific study of consciousness. The five theses include Non-eliminative Materialism (experiences are neurophysiological states of the body), the Two Perspectives View (based in what Feigl calls “Russell-Schlick Monism”), Experiential Embodiment (as recursively self-maintaining systems, subjects of experience engage the world from an embodied perspective, with the details of their embodiment shaping the nature of their conscious minds), Subjective Comprehensibility (the subjective perspective is a comprehensible outgrowth of animal evolution), and the Complex Subject Thesis (the subjects of consciousness are exceedingly complex systems of living matter). All told, the five theses offer a non-deflationary yet naturalistic account of experience, one which mitigates a number of problems and puzzles associated with consciousness, including epiphenomenalism, experiential privacy, and the origins of the subjective perspective. At the same time, the account rules out a number of positions on experience’s relationship to the physical world including various forms of dualism, panpsychism, and platform neutral functionalism.
items.title: Complex Subjects: On the Natural Origins of Subjective Experience

items.abstract: Abstract Delusion is one of the most puzzling doxastic phenomena: on the one hand, the subject appears irrational, holding a delusion despite counterevidence; on the other hand, the subject appears otherwise rational, apportioning their non-delusional beliefs to the evidence. Leading theories of delusion, despite their strengths, still face notable limitations. This article argues that they may benefit from a new empiricist approach. Drawing on insights from Hobbes and Locke, it proposes that the subject may have a distinctive kind of compelling experience that is phenomenologically analogous to, and can effectively be more compelling than, the Cartesian ‘clear experience’. How the experience may, in various ways and to varying degrees, compel domain-specific irrational belief in the face of counterevidence will be articulated.
items.title: Delusions and Compelling Experiences

items.abstract: This paper attempts to dissolve the Gettier problem by employing the notion of background information developed within Bayesian confirmation theory. The paper ultimately defends the traditional Justified True Belief (JTB) analysis of knowledge. The central argument of the paper is that all Gettier cases, as well as several counterexamples to the No False Grounds (NFG) condition, invariably involve falsehood: either the hypothesis itself is false or the justificatory grounds are false, thereby undermining justification. However, in order to identify the precise proposition functioning as the hypothesis or as an evidential statement, and in order to evaluate its truth value, we require a conceptual category called background information . I argue that the failure to specify background information precisely is what prevents epistemologists from identifying the relevant falsehood operative in Gettier cases, whether it concerns a false hypothesis or false justificatory grounds. In many Gettier cases, we fail to recognize that the justified hypothesis is false because two distinct propositions are involved, even though they are expressed by the same sentence. The proposition that is justified is not the same proposition that ultimately turns out to be true. This implicit shift from one proposition to another frequently goes unnoticed because epistemological discussions have largely underestimated the role of background information in determining the proposition expressed by a statement. Every statement, whether explicitly or implicitly, is associated with background information, and changes in the associated background information may alter the proposition expressed by the statement itself. In addition to the notion of background information, the paper also employs the idea of the logical structure of propositions in order to diagnose and dissolve Gettier cases.
items.title: Background Information as a Key to Resolving the Gettier Problem: Insights from Bayesian Confirmation Theory

items.abstract: The aim of this article is to show how infinitariness prowls when metainferences are called into action to solve Carnap’s categoricity problem. We first present the challenge for propositional classical logic, and show whether it could be solved by using three different definitions of metainferential validity. We then discuss some conceptions of metainferences and show some facts about finitary and infinitary metainferential relations, concerning those three definitions. Further, we explore the prospects of retaining finitariness at the expense of weakening the semantics with a third truth value. Finally, we briefly consider the possibility of once more enriching the structure of the theory by taking inferences to be three-sided.
items.title: Infinitary Metainferences, Categoricity and the Structure of Logical Theories

items.abstract: Abstract Doxastic deliberation about how to doxastically relate to a given proposition p is said to be transparent, in that the central deliberative question of ‘Whether to believe p?’ is equivalent to ‘Whether p?’. I discuss four challenges to this thesis based on non-evidential epistemic reasons, deliberative dilemmas, self-effecting attitudes, and permissivist pragmatism. By employing recent insights from both the theory of epistemic normativity and the literature on practical deliberation, I argue that each of these puzzles can be squared with a properly limited and constrained version of the transparency thesis. Ultimately, I show that the claim that doxastic deliberation is after settling ‘Whether p?’ can only be understood as an approximation of a sub-question of the initial normative deliberative question concerning a very specific set of attitudinal options. Nevertheless, the resulting theory retains the core motivation and upshots of the transparency thesis: one is still able to explain why the deliberative norms of doxastic deliberation appear to be, for the most part, epistemic norms.
items.title: Doxastic Deliberation and the Puzzles of Transparency

items.abstract: Abstract We often support our moral judgements by appealing to independent considerations. According to some approaches in moral epistemology, the best way to understand this support is as evidential . However, it is unclear how some metaethical positions, like expressivism, can be compatible with such a view. For expressivists, moral judgements are desire-like states, which ostensibly are not the sorts of states which can be evidentially supported. In this paper, I argue that expressivists can indeed make sense of relations of evidential support for moral judgements. Drawing on a common sides-stepping expressivist strategy, I argue that expressivists should first focus not on evidential relations themselves but on our thought and talk of the form ‘ e is evidence for p ’. I then appeal to a form of epistemic expressivism, according to which such claims express complex non-cognitive attitudes or normative perspectives about standards that make it permissible to judge that p given e . This approach allows expressivists to reinterpret questions about what evidential relations between evidence e and moral judgements that p are as first-order normative questions about which standards not ruled out by acceptable normative perspectives make it permissible to judge that p given e . Responses to these first-order questions should be, in principle, compatible with expressivist second-order accounts of moral thought and talk. Finally, to show that this first-order interpretation is plausible, I outline a version of evidential explanationism along those lines.
items.title: Expressivism and Evidence for Moral Judgments

items.abstract: The Quine-Putnam Indispensability Argument is one of central defenses of traditional mathematical realism, which typically posits a single, determinate universe of mathematical objects. It is debated whether this argument can support mathematical pluralism, the view that multiple mathematical universes exist. Jonas ( 2024 ) argues it cannot, claiming that ontologically isolated universes break the transitive chain of indispensability required for empirical justification. This paper contends that Jonas’s argument is flawed because it conflates ontological isolation with explanatory isolation. We demonstrate that while universes in a multiverse are isolated from one another, they are not explanatorily disconnected. By citing mathematical theorems in analysis that currently require cross-universe proofs, we show that explanatory transitivity persists, thereby allowing a pluralist realism to retain a robust form of indispensability.
items.title: Indispensable Mathematics and Isolated Universes

items.abstract: Abstract Many authors who reject the vacuous truth of counterpossibles still adopt a strangeness of impossibility condition (SIC): possible worlds are always closer than impossible ones. Others doubt that SIC holds across the board. I situate the debate between linguistics and other disciplines. Then I weigh considerations of conservativity, systematicity and intuitiveness against counterexamples to SIC and purported theoretical benefits of abandoning SIC. My result is that neither the supporting nor the opposing evidence so far is compelling. The most plausible hypothesis is that SIC holds for a ‘standard resolution’ of the vagueness of counterpossibles, but that it can be overridden by context and pragmatic considerations even when counterpossibles are assessed ‘out of the blue’.
items.title: Strange Days Have Found Us

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly do more than influence human decision-making; they constrain, block, suspend, and sometimes bypass it. Fraud-detection systems halt transactions, autonomous vehicles override steering and braking, platforms suspend accounts, and emerging neurotechnologies may modulate affective or cognitive states upstream of action. Existing AI ethics has focused primarily on influence, manipulation, fairness, and accountability, but these frameworks do not adequately capture cases in which AI interferes directly with the pathway from a user’s reasons to their action. In this paper, I introduce the concept of digital restraints and argue that their ethics can be illuminated by analogy to the more developed ethics of medical restraints. Drawing on this model, I develop a taxonomy of the moral situations to which restraints respond, and an agency-protective account of permissible digital restraints organized around four conditions: decision-appropriateness, authorization, least agency-restricting means, and heightened scrutiny for reason-bypass. I also extend the dominant model of decisional capacity in medicine to develop an account of decisional capacity in digital contexts, arguing that digital environments can themselves degrade understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and expression. Because authorization is central to the permissibility of restraint, I introduce the concept of Advance Algorithm Directives (AADs) as a mechanism by which users may authorize future AI interventions under specified conditions. The result is a scalar framework for evaluating AI-mediated override across domains that permits AI override while protecting human agency.
items.title: Digital restraints: when AI may override human decisions

items.abstract: Abstract In philosophical work on the ethics of video games, ludic amoralists argue that acts players perform in games are beyond moral scrutiny. This is chiefly supported by the following arguments: the fictional harm argument, the consequentialist rebuttal, and the moral exploration argument. The fictional harm argument supports ludic amoralism in principle: if all game actions are fictional, none can be immoral. The consequentialist rebuttal supports a defeasible default: if violent games do not reliably produce harmful outcomes, amoralism is the default position. The moral exploration argument provides an aesthetic reason for amoralism: play is beyond moral criticism insofar as the player engages with the game in an aesthetic, exploratory way. Drawing on Waltonian theories of fiction, I argue that players often imagine themselves as performing the fictional acts represented in games, ranging from heroic exploits to morally abhorrent deeds. When players do this, they can come to identify with, to varying degrees, their fictional exploits. Strong identification occurs when players interpret their fictional actions as satisfying real desires, such as the desire to harm others. Using examples from players of violent extremist games, as well as mainstream violent games, I show how such identification can arise in practice. Most importantly, I show that in cases of strong identification, all three justifications for ludic amoralism fail.
items.title: Imagining evil: from violent imaginings to violent extremist video games

items.abstract: There is ongoing controversy surrounding what ethical weight, if any, should be given to parents’ reasons in the setting of disagreement about a child’s treatment. Parents often readily explain their decisions without prompting. Yet this is not always the case. Some parents do not want to disclose their reasons, while others may struggle to articulate their reasoning. The question of whether parents have an obligation to share their reasons in pediatric decision-making has received limited attention in the bioethics literature. In this paper, we examine these tensions, aiming to clarify the stakes of reason-seeking and reason-giving practices in pediatrics. First, we briefly summarize prevailing views of parental obligations in philosophical and legal theories of the parental role. Second, we present two strong positions on whether parents have an obligation to share their reasons in pediatric decision-making and consider the implications of each. Third, we propose a more nuanced position that recognizes a pro tanto parental obligation. We offer six guiding considerations (disagreement, capacity concerns, parental discretion/harm to the child, complexity, preference sensitivity, and the burden of enacting the decision on others) and three relational features of decision-making that determine the presence and strength of a parental obligation to give reasons. By mapping the contours of parental reason-giving obligations, we seek to establish a stronger ethical foundation for exploration of the parental role and reasons in treatment disagreements.
items.title: Parental reason-giving obligations in pediatrics: who owes what to whom and why?

items.abstract: Abstract Even if state-led biodiversity conservation projects can result in the displacement, exclusion, and impoverishment of former reserve residents, they are often presented as responding to the public interest. The core idea of these projects, I argue in this paper, is that nature and people should be separated, because people are too dangerous to be part of the landscape. However, this narrow perspective fails to acknowledge the numerous wrongs caused by conservation-induced displacement. That is, considering the interdependent relationships between human and non-human entities at the core of several Indigenous approaches to biodiversity conservation, I show that the conservation-induced displacement of some Indigenous groups can cause three interconnected wrongs: territorial, epistemic, and identity-based.
items.title: Why Conservation-Induced Displacement is Wrong

items.abstract: A number of philosophers reject the view that there are any possible cases in which some feature of the causal history of a person’s vulnerability is a necessary condition for an act of taking advantage of that vulnerability to constitute prima facie wrongful exploitation. I challenge this denial through a series of cases in which a thief falls into a pit and can only be rescued by the person he robbed. The vulnerability or desperation flows directly from the putative exploitee’s own wrongdoing against the would-be exploiter and, depending on the specifics of the case, the transaction fails to constitute prima facie wrongful exploitation even though it bears all the surface marks of prima facie wrongful exploitation. These examples show that, at least in some cases, whether an interaction counts as prima facie wrongful exploitation depends in part on features of the causal history that produced the would-be exploitee’s vulnerability or desperation.
items.title: Against the Anti-History Principle

items.abstract: Abstract Business ethics increasingly explains corporate duties through failure-based theories. The Market Failures Approach (MFA) limits profit-seeking by reference to competitive efficiency, while the Justice Failures Approach (JFA) bars firms from benefiting from unjust background conditions. This article argues that both leave a distinct class of corporate wrongs under-theorized, namely the degradation of relational goods through which corporate authority becomes legitimate and social cooperation remains stable. The article develops a Relational Failures Approach (RFA), according to which firms are relationship-constituting institutions whose permission to exercise discretionary power depends on sustaining relational goods. Drawing on sociology and organizational research, the article defends an empirically grounded and non-perfectionist account of these goods and shows how firms can commit efficiency-compatible, justice-compatible, and institutionally corrosive wrongs. The argument clarifies why familiar corporate pathologies, including disposability regimes and fear-based cultures, are not adequately captured by efficiency or justice alone in contemporary corporate ethics debates.
items.title: Business Firms and Relational Failures: Situating Relational Goods Beyond Market and Justice Failures

items.abstract: Abstract This article draws on the cross-disciplinary literature on risk, uncertainty and precaution to address a central dilemma put forward against precautionary principles. According to this dilemma, weak versions of precautionary principles, which hold that policymakers can justifiably adopt precautionary measures even when they lack certainty of impending harm, fail to justify adopting any precautionary measures. Conversely, strong versions of precautionary principles, which hold that policymakers must adopt precautionary measures whenever they face significant risks of harm, yield contradictory policy prescriptions. The article argues that the proffered defences of precautionary principles provide only a partial solution to this dilemma. The article then demonstrates that a meta-precautionary approach, which applies precautionary reasoning to the prescriptions of precautionary principles, can resolve the dilemma and successfully address further prominent objections put forward against precautionary principles.
items.title: A meta-precautionary solution to the dilemma of precaution

items.abstract: Abstract Autobiographical memory and the self are closely connected. Autobiographical memories provide the information needed to form and maintain a stable self-model (memory-to-self). The self, in turn, modulates the construction of autobiographical memories during retrieval (self-to-memory). Past research has mainly focused on the former direction of influence. However, self-to-memory dynamics are being increasingly investigated both in neurotypical and neurodivergent individuals. We contribute to this line of research in two ways. First, we elaborate on the self-memory system framework focusing on self-related processes involved in autobiographical memory retrieval. In particular, we distinguish between long-term and situationally activated aspects of the self, as well as between its representational and agentive aspects. Second, we propose a general framework for understanding self-to-memory dynamics in major depressive disorder based on four dimensions of the self: self-coherence (comprising self-coherence proper and self-congruence); self-valence; self-knowledge; and self-control. Based on the characteristics of the self in depression, we propose an outline of the self-to-memory dynamics in individuals with depression, drawing on existing empirical evidence. Additionally, we suggest that our framework, adjusted as needed, could be employed to describe self-to-memory dynamics in other mental health conditions.
items.title: Varieties of self-to-memory dynamics in autobiographical memory: the case of depression

items.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework, causal propositional dynamic logic ( CPDL ), grounded in propositional dynamic logic, for reasoning about dependence structures between propositions. We extend this to an epistemic variant–epistemic CPDL –which integrates causal reasoning with propositional knowledge. Our formalism supports a variety of dynamic updates, including fact changes, structural modifications, and epistemic state updates, allowing for the modeling of systems in which both causality and knowledge evolve. For any fixed language of epistemic CPDL , we provide a complete axiomatization and establish the decidability of validity. To demonstrate the flexibility and expressiveness of our approach, we define inverse event operators, formalize sufficient and actual causes, and analyze causal relations among complex propositions. We also present a detailed comparison with the Halpern-Pearl framework, highlighting both conceptual parallels and the syntactic strengths of our logic-based methodology. We conclude by outlining promising directions for future research.
items.title: Towards a PDL Framework for Reasoning About Causality

items.abstract: This paper presents a philosophical and experimental study of fairness interventions in AI classification, centered on the explainability and transparency of corrective methods, and on the opposition between two fairness criteria, namely Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Our main argument is that even as a gap in Demographic Parity is used to diagnose inequality between groups, Equalized Odds constitutes a more reliable fairness criterion to guide bias correction in classification. To establish this, we present FairDream , a fairness package intended for lay users, whose mechanism increases the model’s weights of errors on disadvantaged groups. To justify FairDream ’s results, we analyze its reweighting algorithm, and we present the results of a benchmark experiment in which we compare FairDream with a distinct in-processing correction method that enforces Demographic Parity more drastically, the GridSearch method. We then propose a normative justification of Equalized Odds, with a discussion of the criterion’s limitations. We draw on the structural similarity between FairDream ’s results and a version of Simpson’s paradox to justify conditioning on true labels in counterfactual evaluations of fairness.
items.title: Fairness Interventions in Classification: A Study on AI Explainability

items.abstract: In a recent paper, ‘Transcendental Philosophy As Capacities-First Philosophy’ (Schafer 2021 ), Karl Schafer argues that Kant’s critical philosophy places capacities first in both epistemic and explanatory orders of priority. While Schafer remains neutral on the ultimate specification of the explanatory order, he describes Kant as committed to “some sort of metaphysical dependence of the form of the sensible world on the form of our cognitive faculties ” (2020: 676–677; emphasis in the original). This is his reading of such claims as that “nature itself” is “possible in general in the material sense…by means of the constitution of our sensibility”, and “in the formal sense…by means of the constitution of our understanding” [ Prolegomena 4:318]. In this description Schafer presupposes that the notion of explanatory or metaphysical priority which he uses to articulate the capacities-first position is itself prior to any notion of these capacities. Thus, for Schafer, the capacities-firster applies a notion whose philosophical significance and applicability is not local to the discussion of our capacities and their objects, one with application in metaphysical discussion of other topics. In particular, for Kant to say that our capacities are the ground of the form of the sensible world is to disagree substantively with those who would claim, with equal coherence and intelligibility, that something else is that ground. Footnote 1 My aim in this essay is not to dispute Schafer’s claim. Rather, it is to explore what it would mean to read Kant as taking our capacities to be first in another sense, perhaps compatible with his: not first according to a metaphysical order of priority, where ‘metaphysical’ is understood in the contemporary anglophone sense, but first relative to metaphysics itself, where ‘metaphysics’ is understood in Kant’s sense. Footnote 2 From this point of view, Kant’s explanation of how metaphysics (which is certainly metaphysics in his sense) is possible—one of the principal tasks of his critical philosophy—requires not in the first instance a startlingly idealistic thesis within an unaltered metaphysics but a “seemingly daring” [ Prolegomena 4:320] alteration of the tradition’s understanding of what metaphysics is in the first place, a “better explanation of [its] own nature” [ Prolegomena 4:280]. Footnote 3 This idea has been suppressed on the contemporary interpretive scene, perhaps by the sense, shared by ‘metaphysical’ and ‘methodological’ readers of transcendental idealism alike, that it is obvious what metaphysics is—namely, a matter of the theorist’s commitments to there being something or its having one or another kind of property or standing in one or another kind of relation—and that if Kant’s Metaphysik is not that, then this is a merely terminological matter of little substantive interest. Footnote 4 But the question of the constitutive subject matter of a science (and not merely a set of commitments) called ‘metaphysics’ (and its various cognates) was live in the medieval and early modern period. Early modern German rationalists like Leibniz inherited from Suárez an initially controversial conception of the science as concerned with real being [ ens reale ]. Footnote 5 There are also moments in which they characterize it in terms of a capacity which we possess, as when Leibniz says that it is the “science of intelligible things [ scientia rerum intellectualium ]” ( 1903 : 556), things insofar as they are objects of the intellect. This variation in characterizations of the science is undergirded by an intimate connection between the notions of the real and the intelligible, which are even sometimes asserted to be equivalent, as in the scholastic doctrine of the convertibility of the real and the true, at least as understood by some figures. But where notions are equivalent, there is a question of notional priority. Footnote 6 And it is not always easy to say, for these preKantians, which of these notions is meant to take priority—that of real being or that of an object of the intellect—because it is difficult to catch them explicitly addressing themselves to this question. (They are most often, and certainly by Kant scholars, usually without comment, understood as according priority to real being over intelligibility.) Kant’s conception of metaphysics should, in my view, be understood as a reaction against this tradition with two principal moments. First, he preserves a privileged role for the notion of reality in the constitution of metaphysics but rejects its equivalence to that of the merely intelligible. For Kant, metaphysics concerns the real because, and only because, its constitutive subject matter is the objects of the capacities for empirical cognition and rational action : theoretical and practical cognition as he understands them. Footnote 7 Each of these objects has reality in the sense of explanatory structure . Moreover, the exercise of each of these capacities essentially involves relation not to something merely intelligible, but to the intelligible sensible . In cognizing empirically, I know something which I perceive, and in acting rationally, I do something perceivable by myself and others. Thus not merely the intellect but also the senses are essentially invoked in the characterization of the subject matter of metaphysics, and of the real insofar as a science concerning it is possible. Second, for Kant unlike for the preKantian, it is clear which notion takes priority in the constitution of metaphysics: it is not that of real being but that of the objects of theoretical and practical cognition, so that his metaphysics is unquestionably capacities-first. Kant is led to confront the priority question in a way in which his predecessors are not, precisely because he includes sensibility, the condition of whose objecthood he understands on analogy with Locke’s notion of a secondary quality, in the constitution of metaphysics. Footnote 8 He combines the position, at which he has arrived by 1770, that (i) what we know a priori about objects of sensibility concerns the way in which we represent them, with the position, at which he as arrived by 1781, that (ii) our a priori knowledge is limited to objects of our sensibility in general, with the background position that (iii) metaphysics is an a priori science, so as to yield the conclusion that metaphysics is a science of the intelligible sensible as such , i.e. , as represented by us in the way we represent it in theoretical and practical cognition. Footnote 9 Or so, in any case, I shall suggest in what follows. This essay will not be a comprehensive defense of this suggestion but a programmatic sketch of what it might mean, two (of many) ways in which the text might be approached on its terms, and a plea for its importance as an expression of an aspect of the spirit of Kant’s critical philosophy which, I think, is not perspicuously expressed by the thought that he is committed to generic explanatory or metaphysical relations between our capacities and other things. Footnote 10 In §2 I sketch a notion of notional priority and explain its application in the characterization of sciences and notions developed in them. In §3 I suggest that Kant defines metaphysics in a twofold way in terms of the science of the objects of theoretical and practical cognition. Thus, for Kant, metaphysics is in the first instance the twofold science of the true and the good, and only derivatively that of the real. I consider two ways in which such objects can be characterized—in pre-cognition or post-cognition terms—and explain how Kantian metaphysics might accordingly be understood as pre-cognition capacity-first philosophy or post-cognition capacity-first first philosophy, with two correspondingly different senses in which the real might be understood as derivative of the true and the good. In §4 I briefly address the distinction between the understanding and reason and explain in what sense reason’s objects belong to the subject matter of metaphysics as characterized in §3. In §5 I turn to the distinction between sensibility and the understanding, and correlatively to the thing in itself. §6 concludes with a reflection on the relation of my principal suggestion here to the dispute between ‘metaphysical’ and ‘methodological’ readers of transcendental idealism and on one of the important differences between Kant’s and the contemporary anglophone conception of metaphysics.
items.title: Capacities-First Philosophy as First Philosophy

items.abstract: Abstract Debates about the extended mind and extended cognition typically focus on the boundaries of cognitive processes and the mechanisms responsible for their realization. This paper develops a different perspective, one that foregrounds the role of dispositional properties such as beliefs, capacities, and abilities. According to the dispositional hypothesis, cases of cognitive extension share a common structure: an entity is credited with a dispositional property whose manifestation is realized by a mechanism that extends beyond the boundaries of that entity. This provides a unified way of understanding otherwise disparate cases of cognitive extension. The dispositional perspective also sheds new light on several familiar issues in the active externalist literature, including cognitive bloat and the criteria used to evaluate putative cases of cognitive extension. More generally, it draws attention to the importance of disposition ascription and the identification of disposition bearers: whether a mechanism qualifies as extended depends not simply on whether it crosses an organismic boundary, but on whether it extends beyond the boundaries of the entity credited with the relevant dispositional property. The resulting framework provides a common basis for understanding both natural and artificial forms of cognitive extension.
items.title: Beyond Skin and Skull: A Dispositional Approach to the Extended Mind

items.abstract: Abstract This paper aims to show that a neo-Aristotelian version of capacity-first philosophy of mind is fruitfully applied to a question which is specific to philosophy of psychology, namely: What counts as an adequate explanation in psychology? Drawing on Kenny, Glock and Schellenberg, the paper argues that the neo-Aristotelian capacity view is built around a set of criteria for the classification of capacities. All capacities are classified according to (1) possession-, (2) exercise-, (3) vehicle-, (4) opportunity-, (5) enablement- and (6) successful employment- criteria. These classification criteria are used to reconstruct the process of de-intellectualizing explanations of psychological phenomena. De-intellectualization targets theoretical assumptions about the circumstances in which the various criteria for classifying capacities are satisfied. The capacity approach offers a tool for regimenting the process of de-intellectualization. It also illustrates the contrast between de-intellectualization and Dennett’s homuncular functionalism. Rather than offering nothing more than conceptual clarity for debates about the metaphysics and epistemology of mind, the neo-Aristotelian capacity view explains why de-intellectualizing explanations is a feature of adequate explanations in psychology.
items.title: Capacity-First Philosophy of Psychology

items.abstract: I present a case of perceptual discrimination without phenomenal difference as a problem case for Schellenberg’s capacitism. According to Schellenberg, employing capacities to discriminate and single out particulars not only constitutes perceptual states but also constitutes their phenomenal contents. If so, then there shouldn’t be cases wherein a subject perceives a particular (and so employs a capacity to discriminate and single it out) yet has a phenomenally indistinguishable perceptual state from that of a subject who fails to perceive that particular. After replying to several objections on Schellenberg’s behalf – including much-discussed cases of perception without discrimination – I present the case just described.
items.title: Discrimination Without Phenomenal Difference in Schellenberg’s Capacitism

items.abstract: This paper examines the role of analogy in abductive reasoning within medical and bio-medical practices. Drawing on a Peircean conception of abduction, we argue that hypothesis formation is best understood as a response to an ignorance-problem, oriented toward action, rather than immediate truth or empirical confirmation. Within this framework, we focus on the interplay between abduction and analogy, which we characterize as abduction by analogy . We show that analogical reasoning often functions as a support for the generation and selection of abductive hypotheses, particularly in contexts marked by limited information, resource constraints, and sometimes urgent practical goals, such as medical reasoning and bio-medical research. Like abduction, analogy does not provide evidence or confirmation, nor does it constitute an independent criterion of correctness. Rather, it contributes to the plausibility and relevance of hypotheses by transferring explanatory structures from a source domain to a target domain. This account is illustrated through a historical case study of Lavoisier’s experiments on animal respiration, where an analogy between metal calcination and respiration of animals guides the formulation of hypotheses subsequently subjected to experimental testing. We argue that such abductions by analogy are ignorance-preserving yet methodologically fruitful. The paper concludes that both abduction and analogy resist strict validity criteria and should instead be evaluated in terms of pragmatic virtues, namely their capacity to guide inquiry and generate a coherent course of action.
items.title: Abduction by Analogy in Bio-Medical Inquiry

items.abstract: Abstract Computational or machine ethics examines how morality could be implemented in machines and represented computationally. In the cognitive sciences, different architectures (rule-based and connectionist) have been proposed. Nevertheless, such approaches have limitations when incorporating ethical claims. With the rise of artificial intelligence, new ways of simulating moral expertise seem possible, where chatbots can serve as dialogue partners for moral orientation. However, as I will argue, such systems lack a theoretical grounding in metaethics, as do the former approaches. In order to align such systems ethically and ground them conceptually, a topography of moral competence must be developed. By outlining this topography, I will show some directions for further research and how such systems might enhance us morally.
items.title: Limitations of Computational Morality: Can We Morally Enhance Ourselves via AI?

items.abstract: Physical AI systems act on the world through learned perception and language-conditioned policies. Autonomous vehicles, inspection drones, industrial manipulators, and intelligent camera networks all belong to this class, and all of them strain the division of labour between safety engineering and AI ethics: an embodied system that misclassifies a person commits a fairness failure and a safety failure in the same instant. Functional safety supplies certifiable machinery but recognises only physical injury, while AI ethics names the full range of harms but produces guidance rather than evidence that can block a release. Reviewing both fields and recent frameworks, we find that no existing instrument combines a broad account of harm with release-blocking enforcement for an individual system, and we identify seven specific gaps. We propose ESPA (Ethical and Safe Physical AI assurance), a pipeline of thirteen stages in four phases. Its central method, the Ethical Hazard and Risk Assessment, grades harms on severity, exposure, and redressability to yield Ethical Integrity Levels, for which we specify a calibration procedure with an agreement threshold fixed in advance. Further mechanisms include an Ethical Operating Domain, ethical safe states, red-teaming across language, sensing, and supply-chain surfaces, and drift monitoring, all enforced by a dual-gate rule under which no stage passes without both its safety and its ethics evidence. We illustrate the pipeline on an inspection drone, a public-space camera, and a collaborative manipulator. ESPA is a conceptual framework specified to engineering detail; it has not yet been validated or certified.
items.title: Ethical and safe by construction: a unified assurance pipeline for physical AI

items.abstract: Abstract This comment assesses the evidence from four papers on the development process for four breakthrough drugs or treatments. The comment notes that the papers show all the key breakthroughs in the development process were financed either through the National Institutes of Health or various foundations or charities, not drug companies looking to be compensated through patent monopolies. It argues that this evidence suggests patent monopolies are an unnecessary distortion that results in high drug prices and creates perverse incentives. Expanded public funding could replace patent monopolies, allowing new drugs to be sold at free market prices, ending the problem of high drug prices blocking access.
items.title: What Have We Learned About Incentive Mechanisms?

items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the role of public interest litigation in promoting accountability for AI and automated decision-making (ADM) in Australia. Since ADM regulation faces political and geopolitical headwinds, effective governance will have to rely on the enforcement of existing laws. Drawing on interviews with Australian public interest litigators, technology policy activists, and technology law scholars, the paper positions public interest litigation as part of a larger ecosystem for transparency, accountability, and justice with respect to ADM. The paper explores the tactics and strategies of what one participant described as “retrofitting” old laws to ADM. These go beyond creative legal argumentation to encompass practices of community-building, collaboration on theories of change, canny selection of clients and causes of action, and careful alignment of the interests of stakeholders in litigation. Naturally, the paper also contends with the limits of these strategies, and of the Australian legal system. Where limits are, however, capable of being overcome, the paper presents findings on urgent needs: the enabling institutional arrangements without which effective litigation and accountability will falter. The paper is relevant to law and technology scholars; individuals and groups harmed by ADM; public interest litigators and technology lawyers; civil society and advocacy organizations; and policymakers.
items.title: Retrofitters, pragmatists, and activists: public interest litigation for accountable automated decision-making

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the significance of what Edmund Husserl calls “the paradox of human subjectivity” for the metaphysical realism‐idealism debate in transcendental phenomenology. I distinguish two plausible interpretations of the paradox that are relevant to this debate. I term the first a vicious circle of mutual dependence: the world is characterized as being ontologically dependent on one causally dependent part of the world. I term the second a paradox of bodily self‐constitution: the transcendental subject is defined in such a way that it would be impossible for it to constitute itself as an empirical subject, and yet, in order to constitute the world, it must undergo such a process of self‐objectification. I focus on one prominent version of phenomenology from each side of the realism‐idealism debate, treating them as counterparts insofar as they share three core commitments. I argue that while the main accounts of the subject available to this idealist version generate at least one such paradox, the realist version can explain how one and the same subject is both transcendental and empirical without generating either paradox. My argument therefore provides a substantial prima facie reason to favour this realist version of phenomenology over its idealist counterpart for those who accept their shared commitments and take transcendental phenomenology to have metaphysical implications for the realism‐idealism debate.
items.title: Realism, Idealism, and the Paradox of Subjectivity in Transcendental Phenomenology
